ai.definition: Digital Afterlife Platforms are technological frameworks designed to capture, store, and potentially transfer human consciousness or memories after death into a digital format.
ai.howItWorks: These platforms leverage advanced AI for data collection, analysis, and synthesis of personal data. Quantum computing is used for secure, efficient storage and complex processing tasks. The technology aims to create virtual representations that can be experienced in simulated environments posthumously.
ai.problemSolved: Addressing the ethical and practical challenges of preserving human consciousness after death by providing a means for continued existence or experience through digital mediums.
ai.manufacturing: Involves developing AI algorithms, quantum computing infrastructure, and secure data storage solutions. Requires interdisciplinary expertise in fields such as neuroscience, computer science, and ethics.
ai.buildProcess: Initial stages involve extensive research into consciousness, AI, and quantum computing. This is followed by prototyping and testing with simulated data before moving to pilot projects involving deceased individuals or their proxies.
ai.costDrivers: High initial investment due to cutting-edge technology requirements. Ongoing costs include maintenance of quantum computing hardware, continuous updates in AI algorithms, and ethical compliance measures.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Expected to grow as technological advancements continue and societal acceptance increases, but faces significant regulatory and ethical hurdles.
ai.regulation: Currently unregulated, with potential future regulations expected from governments and international bodies due to privacy and ethical concerns.
ai.risks: Technological risks such as data breaches, hardware failures. Ethical risks include the potential for misuse or exploitation of deceased individuals' data. Societal risks related to acceptance and trust in these technologies.
ai.profitability: Uncertain at this stage given the novelty and complexity of the technology. Potential for high value if successful but also significant financial risk due to development costs and uncertain market demand.
ai.futureDevelopment: Expected advancements in AI, quantum computing, and neurotechnology will drive improvements in platform capabilities and user experiences. Ethical frameworks and regulatory standards are likely to evolve alongside technological progress.

glossary.def: Technological systems aimed at preserving human consciousness or memories posthumously in digital form.
Highly sophisticated artificial intelligence used for data analysis and synthesis.
A type of computing that uses quantum-mechanical phenomena, such as superposition and entanglement, to perform operations on data.

subsystems.name: Tissue preparation and microscopy
subsystems.role: turn a preserved brain into a stack of images fine enough to see every synapse.

subsystems.name: Image analysis and segmentation
subsystems.role: trace every neuron and synapse out of the image stack.

subsystems.name: Parameter measurement
subsystems.role: fill in the numbers the wiring diagram cannot show.

subsystems.name: Biophysical simulation
subsystems.role: run the reconstructed network as a working model.

subsystems.name: State and identity layer
subsystems.role: keep the emulation running continuously and verifiably.

subsystems.name: Interaction interface
subsystems.role: let whatever is running inside receive senses and act.

buildSteps.title: Preserve the tissue
buildSteps.detail: The brain is fixed chemically and stabilised so its structure does not decay during months of imaging.

buildSteps.title: Section and image it
buildSteps.detail: The block is sliced into nanometre-thick layers, each imaged by electron microscope. A human brain at this resolution would generate on the order of an exabyte of data.

buildSteps.title: Reconstruct the wiring
buildSteps.detail: Software traces the membranes and processes in each slice, then stitches slices together. Machine learning does most of it; people correct the mistakes.

buildSteps.title: Find the synapses
buildSteps.detail: Each connection is located and typed — whether it excites or inhibits, and which chemical it uses. This is the slow, uncertain step.

buildSteps.title: Estimate the missing parameters
buildSteps.detail: Wiring alone does not set behaviour. Channel densities and synaptic weights would have to be inferred or measured by other means, which no method can currently do for a whole human brain.

buildSteps.title: Build the model
buildSteps.detail: Each neuron becomes a set of differential equations; each synapse a rule. The result is a model, not a copy — the fidelity depends entirely on steps 4 and 5.

buildSteps.title: Simulate it
buildSteps.detail: The network is run on a supercomputer. Simulating roughly 86 billion neurons is far beyond current machines in real time, so it would run far slower than life.

buildSteps.title: Test it against the person
buildSteps.detail: The only meaningful check is whether the model behaves like the original. That requires records of a living person's behaviour that we cannot currently collect at the needed detail.

buildSteps.title: Sustain and store it
buildSteps.detail: If it worked, the running state would need continuous checkpointing and backups. Note that quantum computing is not a plausible substrate here — storage and simulation are classical, and quantum hardware cannot hold a stable, error-corrected copy of a brain.

prerequisites.why: complete wiring maps exist for the nematode C. elegans and, in 2024, for a fruit-fly brain; a whole mouse, let alone human, map does not.

prerequisites.tech: Non-destructive readout of a living brain's state
prerequisites.why: post-mortem imaging captures structure but destroys the person, and no method reads out synaptic strengths in a living human brain.

prerequisites.tech: A theory linking neural activity to experience
prerequisites.why: we cannot currently say which physical details matter for a person's memories, personality or awareness.
the largest machines simulate a small fraction of a mammalian brain, and never in real time.
electrode arrays read thousands of neurons at most, against tens of billions.

pathway.milestone: partial connectomes of small animals and dense activity recordings from small regions of mammalian cortex
pathway.unlocks: methods for tracing and simulating circuits at a scale far below a whole brain.

pathway.milestone: a complete mouse connectome with measured cell types and connection strengths
pathway.unlocks: the first end-to-end test of whether a mapped circuit, simulated, behaves like the animal.

pathway.milestone: non-destructive, high-resolution recording from living human tissue
pathway.unlocks: capturing the parameters that post-mortem imaging cannot provide.

pathway.milestone: a whole-human emulation, if the measurement and theory problems are ever solved
pathway.unlocks: nothing guaranteed — many researchers argue the required measurements are unattainable in principle, and the question of whether a simulation would be the same person is unresolved philosophy, not engineering.
